clinicalPearls: Presents with sudden, painless unilateral loss of vision, a central scotoma or floaters immediately after a Valsalva-type effort such as heavy lifting, coughing, vomiting, straining or childbirth
The characteristic finding is a well-circumscribed, dome-shaped pre-retinal haemorrhage at the macula lying beneath the internal limiting membrane or posterior hyaloid
The blood may develop a horizontal fluid level as it settles
Vision depends on whether the fovea is obscured by the haemorrhage
The affected eye is otherwise usually healthy, without retinal vascular disease
Optical coherence tomography helps localise the blood to the sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid space
Most cases are managed by observation as the haemorrhage clears spontaneously, with Nd:YAG hyaloidotomy or vitrectomy reserved for dense or persistent bleeding
reference.pathophysiology: A sudden rise in intrathoracic or intra-abdominal pressure against a closed glottis is transmitted to the ocular venous system, producing an abrupt spike in retinal venous and capillary pressure. This ruptures fragile superficial perifoveal capillaries, and blood collects in the potential space beneath the internal limiting membrane or the posterior hyaloid face, typically pooling at the macula.
additionalDifferentials: Haemorrhage from neovascular age-related macular degeneration
Bleeding related to a blood dyscrasia
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundus examination to identify the dome-shaped pre-retinal haemorrhage
Optical coherence tomography to confirm the sub-internal limiting membrane or sub-hyaloid location
A clear history of a precipitating Valsalva manoeuvre
Full blood count and clotting studies if the event is spontaneous or recurrent
B-scan ultrasound when the haemorrhage obscures the fundus view
redFlags: Bilateral or spontaneous haemorrhage without a clear Valsalva trigger, prompting investigation for a bleeding disorder
Dense vitreous haemorrhage obscuring underlying pathology
Features suggesting an underlying retinal vascular disease
reference.prognosis: The outlook is generally excellent, with most haemorrhages clearing spontaneously over weeks to months and full recovery of vision.
pitfalls: Causing unnecessary alarm or over-investigating a self-limiting condition
Missing an underlying bleeding disorder in atypical or recurrent cases
Assuming every pre-retinal haemorrhage is due to Valsalva
Intervening prematurely when observation would allow spontaneous clearance
references: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course: Retina and Vitreous
management: Reassurance and conservative observation, as most pre-retinal haemorrhages clear spontaneously
Advice to avoid further Valsalva-type straining and heavy lifting during recovery
Upright posture to encourage settling of the macular haemorrhage
Nd:YAG or argon laser membranotomy to drain a persistent sub-hyaloid or sub-internal limiting membrane haemorrhage obscuring the fovea
Pars plana vitrectomy for non-clearing, dense or breakthrough vitreous haemorrhage
Investigation of an underlying bleeding tendency, anaemia or hypertension when the event is spontaneous or recurrent
Serial fundus examination and optical coherence tomography to monitor resolution
